title: Mezzanine Finance UK
summary: Silver Oak Capital's mezzanine / junior finance page (search-result title 'Mezzanine Finance UK') sits under the Development menu as 'Mezzanine / Junior Finance'. Per the search tool's summary of the page [b], it describes mezzanine as a junior loan placed behind senior debt where the lender takes a second charge, explains that the second-charge position carries higher risk and therefore a higher interest rate than the senior facility, and gives an example capital stack of roughly 65% senior debt, 10-20% mezzanine and a small developer equity share. Related site pages seen in the same results position stretch senior and whole loans as single-lender alternatives combining senior and mezzanine debt, and the FAQ frames mezzanine as debt (borrower keeps remaining profit) rather than a profit-share. H1, meta description, loan sizes, durations, fees, timescales and process steps for the mezzanine page itself were NOT revealed by any of the 3 searches. Direct fetching was blocked; everything comes from search snippets/summaries.

sections.heading: What is mezzanine / junior finance (as described on the page)
sections.content: [b] Silver Oak describes mezzanine as a junior loan placed behind senior debt, with the lender taking a second charge. [seed, Scotland blog] mezzanine is 'a secondary loan that sits behind senior debt, reducing the developer's equity requirement'. [seed, /types-of-borrowing/] the development finance options listed are senior, stretched senior, mezzanine/second charge and joint venture equity.

sections.heading: Risk and pricing
sections.content: [b] 'Because the Mezzanine lender is in a second charge position, the risk is higher, and therefore the interest rate is higher than the senior facility.' No numeric mezzanine rate was revealed. For comparison, the stretch senior page [b] puts the blended cost of a stretch senior loan at 'typically between 8% and 10% per annum (plus execution fees)'.

sections.heading: Example capital stack
sections.content: [b] The page gives an example capital stack of roughly 65% senior debt, 10-20% mezzanine, and a small developer equity share. [seed, Scotland blog] 'Senior development loans cover a percentage of land purchase and construction costs, typically up to 65-75% of Gross Development Value.'

sections.heading: Mezzanine vs profit share (from /faq/)
sections.content: [b] Mezzanine is presented as debt rather than a profit-sharing partnership, so the borrower keeps the remaining profit. 'If your project is highly profitable, mezzanine finance is usually cheaper than giving away half your profit.'

sections.heading: Alternatives promoted on the site: stretch senior and whole loans
sections.content: [b] Silver Oak promotes stretch senior and whole loans as single-lender options that combine senior and mezzanine debt. [a] The whole-loans page frames mezzanine as a separate layer that sits alongside a bank's senior loan in a high-leverage deal, says Silver Oak has direct relationships with pension funds, hedge funds and private equity managers, and claims a whole loan can cut legal costs because the borrower pays for two sets of lawyers instead of three.

sections.heading: Broker positioning (homepage, seen in same results)
sections.content: [b] The homepage says the firm 'arranges debt on a wide range of real estate and luxury assets transactions across the UK, US, Western Europe and the Middle East through our network of over 800 lenders'. [seed, /property-development-finance/] access to a vast network of senior debt, mezzanine debt and equity lenders; typically narrows to 3 or 4 potential lending partners per deal.
